Ellis observed the access panel at the back of the longcase clock ajar and fresh tool marks around the latch, indicating recent interference with the case.

Thomas Reed entered from his workshop and admitted recent servicing of the clock three days prior (winding and stripping weight-gear to clean pivots) and stated he left the shop just before eleven.
Lucius held a torn scrap whose fibres lay on top of the knuckles and showed no blood transfer; narrator and Lucius concluded it appeared to have been placed after death.

Forensics pried free a false rear shelf and photographed it; a shallow cavity behind the shelf consistent with the size of a small revolver's grip was revealed.

Photographs showed the revolver seated on a thin brass shim, gilding marked with clock oil, with a curled shaving of brass beside it; thread from the movement ran into the cavity and was fastened to a small bent bracket on the gun's trigger-guard.

Narrator records a mechanical hypothesis tying the strike train to the trigger via the thread and bracket, explaining how a timed discharge toward the blotter could occur and how the case could appear latched afterwards.
Thomas, who'd serviced the clock, gave a denial of involvement and stated he had been to service the clock days earlier and left before eleven.
A typed envelope containing a warning about the ivory had a partial latent print lifted from the flap's diagonal crease that forensics described as consistent with Iris Harben.
Inspection suggested the torn scrap in Lucius's hand had been placed afterward: fibres lying on top of the knuckles and no transfer staining consistent with staging.
Mrs. Harben stated she acted to prevent the sale and acknowledged knowing where the ivory was kept.
Inspector Lane announced Mrs. Harben would be formally held pending further inquiries.
